bib.title: A Survey on Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation for Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation in Large Language Models", Yizheng Huang and Jimmy X. Huang (York University). arXiv:2404.10981v2 [cs.IR], 23 Aug 2024. The ACM template is unfilled ("Conference acronym 'XX", 2018), so treat it as a preprint, 2024.

COVERAGE: About 128,000 of 146,023 chars read. That is the full body, pages 1-28, including Tables 1-4, Algorithms 1-4 and Fig. 5 data (extraction lines 1-1375). Skipped: the reference list (lines 1376-1906), skimmed only for origins. There are no appendices. The extraction is clean. The whole paper is a survey with no new experiments. Its only numeric results are Table 4 and Fig. 5, both reproduced from other papers (MIRAGE/MedRAG, eRAG, BERGEN).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: The survey splits RAG into four phases: pre-retrieval (indexing, query manipulation, data modification), retrieval (search and ranking), post-retrieval (re-ranking, filtering) and generation (enhancing, customization). Single-hop and multi-hop pipelines both follow this structure.
  number: none (4 phases)
  setup: Taxonomy over about 45 studies, Fig. 3 and Table 2.
  quote: "this paradigm is structured into four main phases from a retrieval perspective: pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and generation. Both single-hop and multi-hop retrieval approaches, encompassing iterative retrieve-generate cycles, follow this four-phase structure."
  where: Sec 2.2, p4
- Claim: Retrieval quality matters more than generator choice. Smaller models gain more from retrieval, and LLaMA2-7B with retrieval beats LLaMA2-70B closed-book. This is secondhand evidence from BERGEN/eRAG.
  number: none in the text. Fig 5b shows per-model gains of +0.03 to +0.17 (LLMeval), but the extraction does not map the deltas to models.
  setup: BERGEN [114] compares oracle (gold) passages with closed-book, averaged over the KILT QA datasets. eRAG [119] uses NQ with BM25, RetroMAE and SPLADEv3, re-ranked with a DeBERTa-v3 cross-encoder, and T5-small (60M) and T5-base (220M) with FiD.
  quote: "LLaMA2-7B with retrieval outperforms LLaMA2-70B in a closed-book setting, suggesting that retrieval augmentation can make smaller models more competitive." and "retrieval quality has a more substantial impact on RAG performance than the choice of generator, reinforcing the notion that investing in better retrieval strategies often yields more benefits than relying solely on larger LLMs."
  where: Sec 8.2, p24-25
- Claim: On MIRAGE (medical QA, GPT-3.5), retrieval helps a lot on PubMedQA* and BioASQ and not on the exam-style sets. Corpus-retriever alignment matters. On the Wikipedia corpus, PubMedQA* is 26.4-31.0, below the 36.00 closed-book baseline.
  number: Average accuracy is 60.69 with no retrieval. With the PubMed corpus (23.9M docs) it is 69.23 (BM25), 68.20 (Contriever), 64.41 (SPECTER), 69.38 (MedCPT), 70.26 (RRF-2) and 69.71 (RRF-4). With Wikipedia (29.9M docs) it is 57.74 (BM25), 58.08 (Contriever), 55.51 (SPECTER), 58.95 (MedCPT), 60.14 (RRF-2) and 59.14 (RRF-4).
  setup: GPT-3.5 on the MIRAGE benchmark (MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, MedMCQA, PubMedQA*, BioASQ-Y/N). The first row is CoT with no retrieval. Data comes from the MedRAG paper [144], not the survey's own runs.
  quote: "PubMed (23.9M) BM25 72.27± 1.36 63.71± 1.35 55.49± 0.77 66.20± 2.12 88.51± 1.28 69.23" and "None None 72.91 ± 1.35 65.04± 1.34 55.25± 0.77 36.00± 2.15 74.27± 1.76 60.69"
  where: Table 4, p24
- Claim: Fusing more retrievers with Reciprocal Rank Fusion does not always help. On Wikipedia, RRF-2 (60.14) beats RRF-4 (59.14), and the text attributes this to including SPECTER.
  number: 60.14 vs 59.14 (average accuracy)
  setup: Same MIRAGE setup as above.
  quote: "adding more retrievers does not always lead to better outcomes; for instance, excluding SPECTER in RRF-2 on Wikipedia yields better results than RRF-4"
  where: Sec 8.2, p24
- Claim: Higher retrieval Recall@5 goes with higher end-to-end RAG score, and the best combination is SPLADE-v3 plus cross-encoder re-ranking.
  number: none stated. Fig 5a axes run Recall@5 0.6-1.0 against LLMeval 0.60-0.85.
  setup: eRAG on NQ, generator SOLAR-10.7B, retrievers BM25, RetroMAE and SPLADE-v3, each with and without DeBERTa-v3 re-ranking (RR).
  quote: "as retrieval quality improves, LLM performance increases significantly across various models. Notably, re-ranking with SPLADEv3 and DeBERTa-v3 consistently achieves the best results across datasets and metrics."
  where: Sec 8.2, p24
- Claim: eRAG scores each retrieved document by feeding it alone to the LLM and measuring the downstream metric. The authors say this correlates better with downstream RAG performance than human labels or provenance labels, and is cheaper than end-to-end evaluation.
  number: none
  setup: eRAG [119], on KILT. The claim is from eRAG's authors, relayed by the survey.
  quote: "eRAG demonstrates that its document-level evaluation correlates more strongly with downstream RAG performance compared to conventional methods like human annotations or provenance labels."
  where: Sec 7.1, p21
- Claim: Evaluation splits into retrieval metrics (MAP, MRR, NDCG, Precision, Recall, Hit Rate) and generation metrics (EM, F1, BLEU, ROUGE-L). RAG-specific axes are context relevance, answer relevance, faithfulness, noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration and counterfactual robustness. RAGAS defines faithfulness as supported statements divided by total statements.
  number: none
  setup: Table 1 compares RAGAS, ARES, RECALL, RGB, MIRAGE, eRAG and BERGEN.
  quote: "Faithfulness Supported Statements / Total Statements" and "Context Relevance Extracted Sentences / Total Sentences"
  where: Table 1, p20
- Claim: Five retrieval strategies: basic (linear, single pass), iterative, recursive, conditional and adaptive. Algorithms 1-4 give pseudocode. Iterative loops until a stop condition, recursive generates sub-queries per depth, conditional branches on rules, and adaptive adjusts the query from feedback.
  number: none
  setup: Conceptual taxonomy. Examples: Atlas and REPLUG (basic), IRCoT, ITER-RETGEN, RQ-RAG (iterative), SURGE and MemWalker (recursive), CRAG (conditional), FLARE, Self-RAG, DRAGIN (adaptive).
  quote: "while basic RAGs are usually single-hop searches, i.e., they are retrieved only once as generated supplementary material, today's RAGs are mostly multi-hop searches"
  where: Sec 4.2, p11
- Claim: Survey of the literature: most work uses external data, favours multi-hop, and concentrates effort on query manipulation and retrieval. Few studies address customization. Many systems still use BM25 as the retriever.
  number: none
  setup: Table 2 (about 45 studies) and Table 3. The survey's own reading, not a measurement.
  quote: "A preference for multiple-hop over single-hop retrieval was noted, indicating that iterative search rounds generally yield superior results." and "many systems still rely on traditional retrievers like BM25, valued for their efficiency."
  where: Sec 8.1-8.2, p22-23
- Claim: Indexing: the inverted index cannot find semantically related documents without exact terms. Dense-vector indexes are ANN-based and fall into three families: graph (HNSW, FAISS), product quantization and LSH. LSH is rare in RAG.
  number: AiSAQ is reported to keep billion-scale memory at about 10 MB with minor latency increases.
  setup: Descriptive. The AiSAQ figure is secondhand.
  quote: "even with billion-scale datasets, memory usage can be minimized to around 10 MB with only minor latency increases" and "LSH is rarely used in RAG systems compared to graph-based and PQ methods"
  where: Sec 3.1, p6-7
- Claim: Query manipulation is split into expansion (Query2doc pseudo-documents, FiD wider retrieval), reformulation (RQ-RAG rewrite/decompose/disambiguate, Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, FLARE) and prompt-based rewriting (Step-Back, CoK).
  number: none
  setup: Descriptive.
  quote: "pseudo-documents generated by LLMs enhance the original query, effectively bridging the gap between the user's input and the corpus information, which benefits both sparse and dense retrieval systems."
  where: Sec 3.2, p8
- Claim: Re-ranking uses stronger, slower models because the candidate set is small. It comes in unsupervised (In-Context RALM, with BM25 top-k re-scored by LM likelihood), supervised (BERT in Re2G, T5, RankLLaMA, FiD-Light, GenRT) and data-augmented (Promptagator, DKS-RAC) forms. Filtering is distinct from re-ranking and covers Self-RAG reflection tokens, BlendFilter, RECOMP (can emit an empty summary), CRAG (knowledge strips scored by a fine-tuned T5), FiD-TF token filtering, CoK self-consistency and FILCO (STRINC, lexical overlap, CXMI).
  number: none
  setup: Descriptive.
  quote: "pre-trained models with superior accuracy but lower efficiency can be effectively employed due to the limited set of candidate documents available" and "If the retrieved documents are deemed irrelevant, the compressor can generate an empty summary, effectively filtering out unnecessary information."
  where: Sec 2.2.3 p5; Sec 5.2 p17
- Claim: Generation "enhancing" comes in three forms: with the query (RETRO chunked cross-attention, In-Context RALM prepending), with an ensemble (FiD, REPLUG) and with feedback (PRCA, DSP, Selfmem, RECITE).
  number: none
  setup: Descriptive.
  quote: "FiD [58], which encodes multiple retrieved passages independently before fusing them in the decoder"
  where: Sec 6.1, p17-18
- Claim: Noise robustness: Cuconasu et al. report that under some conditions irrelevant documents raise accuracy. Models also answer anyway when retrieval fails (negative rejection), and HyDE pseudo-documents help at a compute cost.
  number: none
  setup: Secondhand, from Sec 9.1.
  quote: "under certain conditions, the inclusion of irrelevant documents can enhance overall accuracy."
  where: Sec 9.1, p26
- Claim: Efficiency concerns: the multi-step pipeline adds latency; hybrid sparse+dense retrieval trades speed for accuracy; deep re-rankers (monoT5, RankLLaMA) are costly; many post-retrieval methods call LLM APIs; chunking, embeddings and re-ranking interact.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 9.2, discussion only.
  quote: "The multi-step nature of RAG workflows—including query classification, retrieval, re-ranking, and generation—adds complexity and latency"
  where: Sec 9.2, p26-27

LIMITS
- It is a survey with no new experiments. All numbers are copied from MedRAG/MIRAGE, eRAG and BERGEN, and the survey adds no setup detail of its own.
- The Fig. 5b deltas (+0.03 to +0.17) have no mapping to models in the extraction, so do not cite them without checking the figure.
- The comparative claims ("iterative search rounds generally yield superior results", "retrieval quality has a more substantial impact") are the authors' reading of a table of studies, not controlled comparisons. The MIRAGE evidence is one domain (medical QA) with GPT-3.5.
- Coverage ends at about early 2024: GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA2 and BM25 era. There is nothing on long-context models, agentic RAG, GraphRAG or late interaction.
- The authors concede the low coverage of customization and the heavy API cost of post-retrieval methods. They also note multimodal RAG as an open area, which they treat only briefly.
- The text does not discuss chunking in depth despite the pipeline framing. It mentions chunking only in Sec 9.2.
- The ACM metadata is unfilled.

BUILDS ON: Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG, credited as the origin); Khandelwal et al. 2020 (kNN-LMs); Gao et al. [38], Zhao et al. [162] and Hu et al. [48] (prior surveys); Zhu et al. [165] (LLMs for IR survey, used for re-ranking categories); Johnson et al. (FAISS) [68]; Malkov and Yashunin (HNSW) [97]; BM25 [116].

CODE: none. Algorithms 1-4 are pseudocode (pp12-15), e.g. Algorithm 1 loop: "while i ≤ N do ... q′←F_pre(q) ... D_i←R(q′,D) ... D′_i←F_post(q′,D_i) ... y_i←G(q′,D′_i) ... if stopping condition met based on y_i then BREAK ... Update q′← UpdateQuery(q,y_i)".

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p3): the unified RAG core concepts with basic workflow. The simple index, retrieve, generate loop.
- Fig 3 (p6): taxonomy tree mapping each technique to a phase. This is the fastest way to see where each named method sits.
- Fig 4 (p10): a typical RAG framework with iterative retrieval.
- Fig 5 (p25): (a) Recall@5 vs RAG performance by retriever and re-ranker on NQ with SOLAR-10.7B; (b) closed-book vs oracle gains by LLM size; (c) eRAG correlation with downstream performance for T5-small and T5-base. All three show retrieval quality driving results more than generator size.
- Table 1 (p20): comparison of evaluation frameworks and their metrics. Table 2 (p22): which RAG stages each study covers.

PROBLEMS: Reference-list pages (about 18,000 chars) were skimmed and not read in full. Table 2 check-marks extract as "!", so the per-study stage columns cannot be recovered from the text. Table 4 colour coding (red and green) is lost. The Fig 5 axis labels extract but the bar values do not. The text has a few citation slips: RECITE is cited as [122] in Sec 6.1 (it is [125]), and Atlas and Rewrite-Retrieve-Read are both cited as [94]. No embedded instructions found. Local text copy is at /tmp/huang.txt (line numbers refer to it).
